\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals---four instance-level (structural and surface agreement) and one per-sample (log-probability, LP)---for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient, using 4B--8B models.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction.
However, quality estimation does not translate to sample selection---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}: despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom, no signal consistently outperforms greedy decoding.
The gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates within an instance by construction; MBR selection with well-aligned utility ($\rho{=}0.52$) fails because instance degeneracy (10--58\% identical outputs) eliminates headroom; and LP carries genuine per-sample information but is compressed to near-ineffectiveness (median range 0.041 nats).
LP selection is inversely associated with degeneracy: at 10\% (Few-NERD), $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$); at 58\% (CoNLL), LP fails.
In the low-degeneracy regime, LP scales with sample budget ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
Closing the gap for structural signals likely requires learned per-sample scoring.
\end{abstract}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation and sample selection in LLM-based NER across four benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction and error flagging.
However, quality estimation does not translate to sample selection, and the gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; MBR selection with well-aligned utility ($\rho{=}0.52$) fails because instance degeneracy (10--58\%) collapses the candidate pool; and LP, the sole per-sample signal, is compressed to near-ineffectiveness (median range 0.041 nats).
LP selection effectiveness is inversely associated with instance degeneracy: at 10\% (Few-NERD), LP achieves $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$); at 21\% (SciERC), $+0.42$~pp ($p{=}0.091$); at 58\% (CoNLL), LP fails.
In the low-degeneracy regime, LP selection scales with sample budget ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy, and supervised combination of all five signals cannot close the oracle gap, confirming the bottleneck is in the feature space.
Whether these patterns persist at 70B+ scales remains open.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications for practitioners.}
For quality estimation, all signals achieve positive $\rho$ across non-collapsed datasets (LP $\rho{=}0.42$ on Few-NERD, VC $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC, EM AUROC${=}0.82$ on CoNLL).
Rankings hold across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}); at the capability boundary (WNUT-17), all signals collapse.
For selection, LP is the only signal achieving significant gains, and only at low degeneracy: $+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD (10\% degeneracy, $p{<}0.001$), $+0.42$~pp on SciERC (21\%, $p{=}0.091$), failure on CoNLL (58\%).
Structural signals uniformly degrade selection regardless of dataset.
RE signal rankings are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
We identify two mechanisms: \textit{instance degeneracy} (affecting consensus-proximity selection) and \textit{LP compression} (affecting per-sample selection).

Within-instance analysis (restricted to non-degenerate instances where F1 varies across samples) reveals that MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} does correlate positively with F1 (SJ median within-instance $\rho{=}0.524$ on SciERC, $0.994$ on CoNLL), and on these instances consensus-proximity selection closes 23\% (SciERC) to 41\% (CoNLL) of the oracle gap.
However, fine-tuned models exhibit pervasive \textit{instance degeneracy}: 21\% of SciERC instances (58\% on CoNLL) produce identical F1 across all $N$ samples, offering zero selection headroom; an additional 13\% (49\% on CoNLL) yield constant utility scores, preventing MBR ranking entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
Instance degeneracy is not an artifact of our setup but a consequence of model capability: the better the model, the less room for selection to add value.
CoNLL (91\% single-sample F1) exhibits 58\% degeneracy; Few-NERD (75\%) shows 10\%; SciERC (66\%) shows 21\%; WNUT-17 (${\approx}$42\%, macro) shows near-zero.
The tension between model quality and selection utility is inherent, though Few-NERD's low degeneracy despite high performance suggests that dataset-specific factors (number of entity types, semantic overlap) also modulate the rate.
Scale ablation confirms this tension: Qwen3-8B shows 21\% instance degeneracy on SciERC vs.\ 10.4\% for the weaker Qwen3-4B, despite comparable within-instance utility correlation ($\rho{=}0.52$ vs.\ $0.55$; Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high}, all consensus-proximity variants consistently fail because degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
On SciERC, LP selection approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$; $\Delta{=}{+}0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}); on Few-NERD, where degeneracy drops to 10\%, LP achieves significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}), confirming that degeneracy is the gating factor for LP selection.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Instance degeneracy statistics ($T{=}1.0$). ``Constant F1'': all $N$ samples receive identical instance-level F1. ``Constant utility'': MBR (SJ) utility identical across candidates. 4B data confirms degeneracy scales with model capability.}
\label{tab:degeneracy}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
& \shortstack{SciERC 8B\\($N{=}8$)} & \shortstack{SciERC 4B\\($N{=}8$)} & \shortstack{CoNLL 8B\\($N{=}16$)} \\
\midrule
Constant F1 & 21\% & 10.4\% & 58\% \\
Constant utility & 13\% & 7.0\% & 49\% \\
Oracle gap closed (non-deg.) & 23\% & 25.2\% & 41\% \\
Within-inst.\ SJ $\rho$ (median) & 0.524 & 0.550 & 0.994 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, is severely compressed: median LP range is 0.041 nats (IQR [0.024, 0.073]; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with pooled within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){=}0.248$ confirming weak but positive signal.

\paragraph{Non-tied subset analysis.}
Where compression is mitigated, LP selection works.
Restricting to instances with LP range ${\geq}0.05$ ($n{=}210$, 40\% of total; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}), within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied), and LP selection outperforms greedy by $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$).
The effect grows monotonically with $\varepsilon$ (full sweep in Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}), and the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ result survives Bonferroni correction over 5 comparisons.
This demonstrates that LP \textit{does} carry per-sample discriminative information; compression, not signal absence, is the bottleneck.
However, the effect size is sensitive to subset definition, and the non-tied subset constitutes only 40\% of instances, limiting practical impact.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small

\label{tab:nontied_main}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}

\midrule

Stratifying by voting confidence reveals a complementary pattern: high-consistency instances (Q4) have collapsed headroom (4.78~pp), leaving nothing to select, while low-consistency instances retain headroom but unreliable LP rankings (Appendix~\ref{app:vc_quartile}).

\paragraph{$N$-scaling and temperature.}
LP selection improves with $N$, reaching $+0.52$~pp at $N{=}16$ on Few-NERD (paired $p{=}0.003$; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).
On SciERC, even at $N{=}32$ the best signal captures less than 5\% of available headroom (Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection}).
Oracle headroom increases with temperature ($+7.8$~pp at $T{=}0.5$ to $+13.3$~pp at $T{=}1.0$; Table~\ref{tab:t_ablation}), but selection gains remain negligible, isolating the bottleneck at the within-instance ranking mechanism.
A verbalized confidence baseline confirms that score compression is not LP-specific: the model's self-rated confidence clusters at 8\textendash 9/10 (CoNLL mean 9.24, std 1.32), exhibiting the same top-biased pattern regardless of output format (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}; \citealp{bhattacharyya2026beyond}).
The free-form RE ablation ($+2.35$~pp, $p{=}0.025$; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}) indicates format constraints contribute to compression in other task types, though NER's own free-form ablation (std ratio 0.97) isolates this as not the primary cause for NER.
LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to improve over greedy (best: $+0.2$~pp, $p{>}0.3$); an oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming that per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it.
Full $N$-scaling, temperature, verbalized confidence, and signal combination analyses are in Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, and~\ref{app:vc_quartile}.

\paragraph{Hypotheses for LP compression.}
We identify four (non-mutually-exclusive) mechanisms, though we do not isolate their individual contributions.
Two are \textit{constraint-imposed}: (b) schema-dominated tokens, where constrained decoding enforces structural tokens that carry no extraction information yet dominate the sequence; and (c) vocabulary restriction, where constrained decoding shrinks the effective vocabulary, concentrating probability mass.
Two are \textit{model-learned}: (a) token-level averaging, where mean log-probability over long sequences smooths token-level variance; and (d) format-token dilution, where fine-tuned models assign extremely high LP to schema tokens, diluting the signal from entity-name tokens (free-form parse rates of 99.95\% confirm format tokens dominate).
The constraint-imposed mechanisms (b)\textendash (c) predict that free-form decoding should reduce compression; our NER ablation finds negligible change (std ratio 0.97; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), suggesting the model-learned mechanisms (a) and (d) are the primary drivers for NER.

\paragraph{Ablation: free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
Removing grammar constraints (SciERC NER, Qwen3-8B, 4 seeds) yields nearly identical LP distributions (std ratio 0.97) and negligible selection changes (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), ruling out constrained decoding as the cause of NER compression.
Removing format constraints restores LP selection for RE: bootstrap mean $+2.35$~pp (95\% CI [$+0.24$, $+4.50$], $p{=}0.025$, $n{=}397$), though driven by magnitude asymmetry rather than instance-level win rate (sign test: 45W/45L/307T; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
LP selection failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard${=}0.42$; Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}), indicating a systematic rather than stochastic failure mode.
VC tends to select the most typical rather than the best output, consistent with MBR's known mode-seeking bias \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}.
All consensus-proximity strategies fail because instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).

\paragraph{Ablation: entity-token LP.}
We directly test hypothesis (d) by isolating entity-mention tokens from the log-probability computation.
On SciERC, entity-token LP exhibits $4{\times}$ higher within-instance variance than full-sequence LP, confirming that format tokens do compress the signal.
However, entity-token LP selection performs strictly \textit{worse} than full-sequence LP on both datasets ($-2.0$~pp on SciERC, $-3.3$~pp on CoNLL).
Entity tokens are either too sparse (5.3\% of sequence tokens on SciERC) for stable estimation, or nearly saturated (79.4\% of instances tied on CoNLL), consistent with CoNLL's limited entity vocabulary (4 types, high-frequency names) that fine-tuning drives to near-deterministic prediction.
This rules out format-token dilution as the primary cause and points to an intrinsic pattern: fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities to entity-name tokens themselves, leaving minimal discriminative signal regardless of aggregation scope.
Even disaggregating to entity-token logprobs fails to break compression: on CoNLL, 79.4\% of sample pairs share identical entity-token LP, confirming that compression operates at the representation level rather than being diluted by non-entity tokens.

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
The correlation-selection gap for structural signals is persistent across all four datasets, but LP selection is degeneracy-gated.
At the \textit{low-resource boundary} (WNUT-17, macro F1${\approx}$42\%), QE signals themselves become unreliable: full-set correlations are dominated by the zero/non-zero boundary (VC conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}), so selection is moot.
At the \textit{ceiling boundary} (CoNLL, F1${\approx}$91\%, 58\% degeneracy), selection shows only a marginal structural exception: VC achieves $+0.28$~pp ($p{<}0.03$) at $N{=}16$, capturing ${\sim}$10\% of the 2.5~pp oracle headroom (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}); LP fails entirely.
In the \textit{moderate regime}, instance degeneracy determines LP effectiveness: at 21\% degeneracy (SciERC), LP gains are positive but sub-significant ($+0.42$~pp, $p{=}0.091$); at 10\% degeneracy (Few-NERD), LP achieves highly significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}).
The cross-dataset gradient (58\% $\to$ fail, 21\% $\to$ weak, 10\% $\to$ strong; $n{=}3$ datasets) is consistent with degeneracy below ${\sim}$15\% being a necessary condition for LP selection; entity-type-level evidence provides stronger statistical grounding (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$, $n{=}8$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
When candidates differ sufficiently in quality, LP's per-sample signal can exploit the headroom.
The pattern persists at finer granularity: per-entity-type analysis on Few-NERD shows 7/8 types with positive LP gains, the sole exception being the highest-degeneracy type (Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy because they rank candidates by typicality, not quality.
Whether these patterns persist on larger models (70B+) remains open.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.
Even supervised combination of all five signals (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) fails to close the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}), confirming the information bottleneck is in the signal space accessible to unsupervised aggregation (our five hand-crafted features); whether richer per-token representations (e.g., hidden-state probes) can close the gap is an open question.
Effective selection thus requires content-aware verifiers that examine output semantics \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}, not confidence signal aggregation; $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
Practitioners should estimate instance degeneracy on a small held-out set before deploying multi-sample selection.
Below ${\sim}$15\% degeneracy, LP-based selection yields ${\sim}$1\textendash 2~pp gains and scales with $N$; above ${\sim}$20\%, selection adds no value and greedy decoding is preferred.
Few-NERD's results represent the first demonstration that confidence-based selection \textit{can} succeed for structured IE when degeneracy conditions are met.
The degeneracy diagnostic requires only one generation pass per instance (counting how often samples produce identical outputs); no additional model calls are needed.
Multi-sample inference incurs $N{\times}$ compute; for quality estimation alone ($\rho$ up to 0.45), $N{=}8$ suffices (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}), making the cost acceptable for selective prediction in high-stakes IE.

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
3	We evaluate five confidence signals (four instance-level, one per-sample log-probability [LP]) for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient, using 4B\textendash 8B models.
4	All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD), supporting selective prediction.
5	Quality estimation does not translate to sample selection, however: despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom, no signal consistently outperforms greedy decoding.
6	The gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates within an instance by construction; Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) selection with well-aligned utility ($\rho{=}0.52$) fails because instance degeneracy (10\textendash 58\% identical outputs) eliminates headroom; and LP is compressed to near-ineffectiveness for constrained-format NER (median range 0.041 nats).
7	LP selection is inversely associated with degeneracy: at 10\% (Few-NERD), $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$); at 58\% (CoNLL), LP fails.
8	In the low-degeneracy regime, LP scales with sample budget ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
9	Closing the gap for structural signals likely requires learned per-sample scoring.
10	\end{abstract}
